q: Virtual Reality is best defined as:
options: A 2D game viewed on a monitor
A computer-generated simulation that replaces the user's sensory input with a synthetic 3D environment
A photo-editing filter applied to a live camera feed
A method of compressing video files
explanation: A computer-generated simulation that replaces the user's sensory input with a synthetic 3D environment

q: What happens when a VR user turns their head, unlike watching a monitor?
options: More of the synthetic world is revealed instead of the screen's edge
explanation: More of the synthetic world is revealed instead of the screen's edge

q: Immersion, as used in this course, refers to:
options: A subjective feeling of being present
The objective, technical degree to which a system replaces real sensory input with synthetic input
explanation: The objective, technical degree to which a system replaces real sensory input with synthetic input

q: Presence is best described as:
options: The subjective psychological feeling of 'being there'
explanation: The subjective psychological feeling of 'being there'

q: Interactivity in a VR system means:
options: The environment responds in real time to the user's actions and viewpoint
The app can be updated over the internet
explanation: The environment responds in real time to the user's actions and viewpoint

q: Why must VR frames typically render at 90 Hz or more?
options: To sustain real-time rendering fast enough to avoid breaking the illusion
explanation: To sustain real-time rendering fast enough to avoid breaking the illusion

q: A headset with a wide field of view and high resolution but poor tracking would most likely have:
options: High immersion but potentially low presence
No presence and no immersion, by definition
explanation: High immersion but potentially low presence

q: Which statement captures the classic 'immersion vs presence' distinction?
options: Immersion is psychological; presence is technical
Immersion is technical/objective; presence is subjective/psychological
They are interchangeable terms with no difference
Presence only exists in augmented reality
explanation: Immersion is technical/objective; presence is subjective/psychological

q: The Reality-Virtuality continuum was first described by:
explanation: Milgram & Kishino in 1994

q: On the Reality-Virtuality continuum, which end represents the fully physical world?
explanation: Real Environment

q: Which end of the Reality-Virtuality continuum is fully synthetic?
explanation: Virtual Reality

q: Where does Mixed Reality sit on the Reality-Virtuality continuum?
options: It spans the middle of the continuum
Only at the fully virtual end
It is not part of the continuum
explanation: It spans the middle of the continuum

q: Augmented Reality (AR) is best characterized as:
options: A fully synthetic environment with no real-world reference
Real world view with digital overlays added on top
A headset that blocks out the real world entirely
explanation: Real world view with digital overlays added on top

q: A typical example device for experiencing AR mentioned in the course is:
explanation: A phone camera with filters

q: Mixed Reality (MR) differs from simple AR because MR:
options: Anchors and occludes digital objects relative to real ones
explanation: Anchors and occludes digital objects relative to real ones

q: Which device is given as an example of Mixed Reality in the course material?
explanation: Meta Quest 3 passthrough

q: Virtual Reality (VR), as placed on the continuum, means:
options: A partially real, partially synthetic scene
A fully synthetic environment with the real world blocked out
A 2D overlay on a live camera feed
explanation: A fully synthetic environment with the real world blocked out

q: Which two game engines does the course primarily use for native VR apps?
explanation: Unity and Unreal Engine

q: Which technology is used in the course for browser-based VR that needs no install?
explanation: WebXR

q: Standalone headsets such as the Meta Quest run internally on which operating system base?
explanation: Android

q: When building for Quest in Unity, which platform module must be enabled that first-timers often miss?
options: The Android build platform with XR Plug-in Management
explanation: The Android build platform with XR Plug-in Management

q: Why does the course recommend OpenXR over vendor-specific SDKs like Oculus Integration when possible?
options: OpenXR is the industry-standard cross-platform API, letting one build reach multiple headsets
OpenXR only works with Unreal Engine
OpenXR removes the need for controllers
explanation: OpenXR is the industry-standard cross-platform API, letting one build reach multiple headsets

q: In Unity, what does right-clicking in the Hierarchy and choosing XR > XR Origin (VR) create?
options: A single prefab giving a tracked head camera and two tracked hand controllers
explanation: A single prefab giving a tracked head camera and two tracked hand controllers

q: Which Unity package is essential to install first for a new VR project, per the course's package manager steps?
explanation: com.unity.xr.interaction.toolkit

q: Which of these is NOT one of the four properties described as core to VR in Module 01?
explanation: Compression ratio

q: According to the course, professional VR content is usually built:
options: From scratch using raw graphics APIs
In a game engine rather than from scratch
Exclusively in a web browser console
explanation: In a game engine rather than from scratch

q: What best distinguishes VR from a traditional video game played on a monitor?
options: VR surrounds the user so turning the head reveals more world, not a screen edge
VR requires a mouse and keyboard
explanation: VR surrounds the user so turning the head reveals more world, not a screen edge

q: An AR filter applied through a phone's camera app is an example of where on the Reality-Virtuality continuum?
options: Near the Real Environment end, on the AR side
Exactly at the Virtual Reality end
explanation: Near the Real Environment end, on the AR side

q: Which statement about Unreal Engine's role in this course is accurate?
options: It is used only for 2D mobile games
It is used alongside Unity for building native VR apps
It cannot build for VR headsets
explanation: It is used alongside Unity for building native VR apps

q: The course frames 'a common interview trap' around which two terms?
explanation: Immersion and presence

q: Which of the following is closest to the definition of real-time rendering in a VR context?
options: Rendering a movie file offline before playback
Generating frames fast enough, typically 90Hz+, to avoid breaking the illusion
Rendering only when the user presses a button
Pre-rendering all possible frames in advance
explanation: Generating frames fast enough, typically 90Hz+, to avoid breaking the illusion

q: Which is an accurate pairing from the AR/MR/VR comparison table in the course?
options: VR = real world with digital overlays
AR = real world with digital overlays
MR = fully synthetic environment with the real world blocked out
VR = digital objects anchored to real ones
explanation: AR = real world with digital overlays

q: A first-time Unity XR developer forgets to enable a required module and their Quest build fails to launch in VR mode. What likely went wrong?
options: They forgot to enable XR Plug-in Management for Android
They used C# instead of Blueprints
explanation: They forgot to enable XR Plug-in Management for Android

q: Why is WebXR highlighted as useful for user-facing distribution in Module 01?
options: It requires the most powerful GPU available
It lets an experience run in-browser with zero install for the user
It replaces the need for a headset entirely
explanation: It lets an experience run in-browser with zero install for the user

q: Degrees of Freedom (DOF) describe:
options: Only how bright a display can get
How many independent ways an object or head can move in space
The battery capacity of a headset
explanation: How many independent ways an object or head can move in space

q: 3DOF tracking captures which kind of movement?
explanation: Rotation only (pitch, yaw, roll)

q: 6DOF tracking captures:
explanation: Both rotation and physical translation (position)

q: Which device is given as an example of a 3DOF headset?
explanation: Google Cardboard

q: Which devices are given as examples of 6DOF headsets?
options: Google Cardboard and early Gear VR only
explanation: Quest 3, Valve Index, and PSVR2

q: Why are nearly all modern consumer headsets 6DOF for both head and hand controllers?
options: To let users physically duck behind cover or reach out and grab objects at the correct distance
Because 3DOF is no longer legal to manufacture
Because 6DOF requires no sensors at all
explanation: To let users physically duck behind cover or reach out and grab objects at the correct distance

q: Roughly how wide is human peripheral vision, per the course?
explanation: 200-220 degrees

q: Most consumer headsets cover a field of view of approximately:
explanation: 90-120 degrees

q: VR display resolution is usually reported:
options: As a single combined number for both eyes
explanation: Per eye, not combined

q: The screen-door effect refers to:
options: Visible gaps between pixels at low pixels-per-degree (PPD)
A physical latch on the headset strap
explanation: Visible gaps between pixels at low pixels-per-degree (PPD)

q: Foveated rendering works by:
options: Rendering everything at maximum sharpness always
Rendering sharp detail only where eye-tracked gaze lands, blurring the periphery
Disabling rendering entirely to save power
Increasing resolution uniformly across the whole frame
explanation: Rendering sharp detail only where eye-tracked gaze lands, blurring the periphery

q: What is motion-to-photon latency?
options: The battery life of a headset
The time between a physical head movement and the corresponding pixel updating on screen
The delay in spatial audio only
The time to boot the headset
explanation: The time between a physical head movement and the corresponding pixel updating on screen

q: Above roughly what latency do users start to notice lag that causes discomfort?
explanation: 20ms

q: What is the single biggest cause of VR discomfort, according to the course?
options: Mismatch/lag between head movement and the corresponding display update
explanation: Mismatch/lag between head movement and the corresponding display update

q: Asynchronous Timewarp (ATW) works by:
options: Increasing the field of view artificially
Re-projecting the last rendered frame using the newest head-pose data right before display
Adding motion blur to hide dropped frames
explanation: Re-projecting the last rendered frame using the newest head-pose data right before display

q: Asynchronous Spacewarp (ASW) is used when:
options: The app can't sustain the target frame rate, so an interpolated frame is synthesized
explanation: The app can't sustain the target frame rate, so an interpolated frame is synthesized

q: Typical target frame rates for VR apps, compared to flat-screen games, are:
options: Higher, around 72-120 FPS depending on headset
Irrelevant, since VR does not use frame rate
explanation: Higher, around 72-120 FPS depending on headset

q: Why are dropped frames especially problematic in VR compared to flat-screen games?
options: They are only a cosmetic issue in VR
They are felt physically, not just seen
They have no measurable effect in VR
explanation: They are felt physically, not just seen

q: VR motion sickness generally stems from:
options: A mismatch between what the eyes report and what the vestibular (inner ear) system feels
explanation: A mismatch between what the eyes report and what the vestibular (inner ear) system feels

q: The vergence-accommodation conflict occurs because:
options: The eyes converge to focus on a nearby virtual object but must accommodate to a fixed physical lens distance
The headset battery drains too quickly
The controllers vibrate at the wrong frequency
explanation: The eyes converge to focus on a nearby virtual object but must accommodate to a fixed physical lens distance

q: Vergence-accommodation conflict is primarily associated with:
options: Eye strain over long VR sessions
explanation: Eye strain over long VR sessions

q: Vignetting, as a comfort technique, works by:
options: Increasing color contrast at the center of the screen
Narrowing/darkening peripheral vision during fast artificial locomotion
explanation: Narrowing/darkening peripheral vision during fast artificial locomotion

q: Teleportation locomotion is used as a comfort mitigation because:
options: An instant position swap avoids the smooth-slide sensation that can trigger motion sickness
It requires no tracking at all
explanation: An instant position swap avoids the smooth-slide sensation that can trigger motion sickness

q: A fixed horizon reference (like a stable cockpit or floor grid) helps reduce motion sickness by:
options: Providing a stable visual anchor point
Removing the need for head tracking
explanation: Providing a stable visual anchor point

q: Snap turning is a comfort technique that:
options: Rotates the camera continuously and smoothly
Rotates the view in discrete steps rather than continuously
explanation: Rotates the view in discrete steps rather than continuously

q: Why must sound in VR be 3D-positional?
options: So it correctly changes in loudness/phase as a sound source moves relative to the tracked head, preserving the illusion
Because stereo audio is not supported in headsets
explanation: So it correctly changes in loudness/phase as a sound source moves relative to the tracked head, preserving the illusion

q: What do Head-Related Transfer Functions (HRTFs) model?
options: How the shape of the ear filters sound arriving from different directions
How lenses magnify a display panel
explanation: How the shape of the ear filters sound arriving from different directions

q: Why is spatial audio called one of the 'cheapest immersion upgrades'?
options: It requires no coding at all
It costs relatively little GPU/CPU budget but strongly reinforces presence
It eliminates the need for a display
It is free to license in every engine
explanation: It costs relatively little GPU/CPU budget but strongly reinforces presence

q: Which comfort technique involves a curved ray and a landing reticle rather than a smooth slide?
explanation: Teleportation locomotion

q: Which of the following pairs a DOF type with its correct capability?
explanation: 3DOF: rotation only; 6DOF: rotation + position

q: A headset that can only track where the user is looking but not their physical lean or step is best described as:
explanation: 3DOF

q: Which technique reprojects an already-rendered frame using the very latest head pose right before it is displayed?
explanation: Asynchronous Timewarp

q: A user reports eye strain after long sessions focusing on nearby virtual objects, but the headset optics are correctly calibrated. This is most likely explained by:
explanation: Vergence-accommodation conflict

q: Which four components make up the core anatomy of a VR headset described in the course?
options: Battery, SIM card, antenna, charger port
CPU, RAM, hard disk, power supply
explanation: Displays, lenses, cameras/sensors, IMU

q: In a headset's display system, each eye typically sees:
options: A slightly different virtual camera view for that eye
A black screen at all times
explanation: A slightly different virtual camera view for that eye

q: What is the role of Fresnel or pancake lenses in a headset?
options: To magnify a close display panel to fill the field of view
To capture outward-facing video for passthrough
explanation: To magnify a close display panel to fill the field of view

q: Outward-facing cameras/sensors on a headset are primarily used for:
explanation: Inside-out tracking and passthrough video

q: The IMU (accelerometer + gyroscope) in a headset is sampled at what rate for fast rotational tracking?
explanation: 1000Hz or more

q: Which display panel type is described as cheap, bright, and free of burn-in risk, but with lower contrast?
explanation: Fast-switch LCD

q: Which display technology offers true blacks and high contrast, but is more expensive and carries burn-in risk?
explanation: OLED

q: Pancake lens + Mini-LED combinations are primarily valued for:
explanation: Much thinner headset form factor

q: How do pancake lenses achieve a thinner headset compared to Fresnel lens designs?
options: They fold light back and forth between two lens elements instead of one long lens
They use mirrors mounted outside the headset
They project directly onto the retina
explanation: They fold light back and forth between two lens elements instead of one long lens

q: Which headsets are cited as examples that became noticeably slimmer using pancake lenses?
options: HTC Vive original and Valve Index
explanation: Quest 3 and PSVR2

q: Outside-in tracking relies on:
options: Cameras mounted only on the headset itself
External base stations or cameras placed around the room observing the headset
explanation: External base stations or cameras placed around the room observing the headset

q: A key trade-off of outside-in tracking (like SteamVR Lighthouse) is:
options: Very high precision but requires room setup with external hardware
It cannot track controllers, only heads
explanation: Very high precision but requires room setup with external hardware

q: Inside-out tracking computes headset position by:
options: Using cameras on the headset itself to watch the room via SLAM
explanation: Using cameras on the headset itself to watch the room via SLAM

q: A downside of inside-out tracking mentioned in the course is:
options: It can lose tracking in low light or featureless rooms
explanation: It can lose tracking in low light or featureless rooms

q: Which headsets are given as examples of inside-out tracking?
options: Valve Index and SteamVR base stations
Meta Quest and Apple Vision Pro
explanation: Meta Quest and Apple Vision Pro

q: A typical 6DOF controller combines which components, per the course?
options: IMU, tracked LED/camera markers, capacitive touch sensors, haptic actuator
Only a single button and a battery
A GPS chip and a barometer
A microphone and a speaker only
explanation: IMU, tracked LED/camera markers, capacitive touch sensors, haptic actuator

q: Capacitive touch sensors on VR controllers are used to:
options: Detect finger position without requiring a full button press
explanation: Detect finger position without requiring a full button press

q: Why do newer headsets increasingly favor camera-based hand tracking for casual interactions?
options: It eliminates the need for any tracking system
It offers controller-free finger tracking convenient for light interactions
It provides better haptic feedback than physical controllers
It is required by law in most countries
explanation: It offers controller-free finger tracking convenient for light interactions

q: For fast-paced gaming tasks like shooting, why are physical controllers often still preferred over hand tracking?
options: Haptic feedback and button latency still matter for precision tasks
Hand tracking is banned in competitive gaming
Physical controllers use less battery than hand tracking
Hand tracking cannot detect any movement at all
explanation: Haptic feedback and button latency still matter for precision tasks

q: According to the headset comparison table, Meta Quest 3 is noted for:
options: OLED with eye tracking and HDR
explanation: Best price/ecosystem balance

q: According to the headset comparison table, the Valve Index is notable for:
options: Being fully standalone with no PC tether
Finger-tracking 'knuckle' controllers on a PC-tethered system
Passthrough MR as its primary feature
Being the cheapest headset on the market
explanation: Finger-tracking 'knuckle' controllers on a PC-tethered system

q: According to the headset comparison table, PSVR2 is notable for:
options: Inside-out tracking, OLED with eye tracking and HDR, PS5-tethered
Standalone operation with no console needed
Being tethered to a PC only
explanation: Inside-out tracking, OLED with eye tracking and HDR, PS5-tethered

q: According to the headset comparison table, Apple Vision Pro is notable for:
options: A dense inside-out sensor array, Micro-OLED, and an MR-first design
Being the lightest headset with no battery
explanation: A dense inside-out sensor array, Micro-OLED, and an MR-first design

q: Which tracking type does the Valve Index use?
explanation: Outside-in Lighthouse

q: Which of these headsets is standalone with PCVR as an optional extra, per the comparison table?
explanation: Meta Quest 3

q: A screen-door effect complaint from a user is most directly related to which hardware factor?
options: Low pixels-per-degree (PPD) on the display panel
explanation: Low pixels-per-degree (PPD) on the display panel

q: Which headset component is most directly responsible for fast, low-latency rotational tracking between full pose updates?
explanation: The IMU (accelerometer + gyroscope)

q: If a headset needs external base stations placed around the room to function, it is using:
explanation: Outside-in tracking

q: A headset advertised with 'MR-first design' and a dense inside-out sensor array most closely matches which device in the comparison table?
explanation: Apple Vision Pro

q: Which is a correct strength/weakness pairing from the display technology table?
options: OLED: cheap and no burn-in risk
Fast-switch LCD: true blacks, high contrast
Pancake lens + Mini-LED: much thinner form factor but narrower optical sweet spot
Fast-switch LCD: highest cost of the three
explanation: Pancake lens + Mini-LED: much thinner form factor but narrower optical sweet spot

q: Why would a developer choose OLED over fast-switch LCD despite the higher cost?
options: OLED offers true blacks and higher contrast
OLED is immune to all burn-in risk
OLED is always cheaper to manufacture
explanation: OLED offers true blacks and higher contrast

q: Which statement about controller haptics is accurate?
options: Haptic actuators provide vibration feedback as part of the controller hardware
Haptic actuators are only found in headsets, never controllers
Haptics have been fully replaced by hand tracking in all headsets
Haptics are unrelated to controller design
explanation: Haptic actuators provide vibration feedback as part of the controller hardware

q: A room with poor lighting and few visual features would most challenge which tracking approach?
options: There is no tracking approach affected by lighting
explanation: Inside-out tracking

q: Where do VR engines typically place the coordinate origin?
options: At the ceiling of the room
At a real-world reference point, often floor level at the center of the play space
At the location of the nearest window
explanation: At a real-world reference point, often floor level at the center of the play space

q: Which coordinate system convention does Unity use by default?
explanation: Left-handed, Y-up

q: Which coordinate system convention does Unreal Engine use by default?
explanation: Left-handed, Z-up

q: Most math and graphics textbooks conventionally use which coordinate handedness?
explanation: Right-handed

q: Why is coordinate handedness a frequent source of bugs?
options: Engines differ (e.g., Unity vs. Unreal vs. textbooks), causing issues when porting code between them
It only affects audio, not visuals
Handedness has no practical effect on development
explanation: Engines differ (e.g., Unity vs. Unreal vs. textbooks), causing issues when porting code between them

q: A tracked object's pose is represented every frame as a Transform, which consists of:
options: A position vector plus a rotation
explanation: A position vector plus a rotation

q: Parenting an object to the XR camera rig allows a child object (like a held weapon) to:
options: Automatically inherit the head or hand's position
explanation: Automatically inherit the head or hand's position

q: What is gimbal lock?
options: A physical lock on the headset strap
A state where two rotational axes align and a degree of freedom is lost, occurring with Euler angles
A security feature preventing unauthorized app installs
explanation: A state where two rotational axes align and a degree of freedom is lost, occurring with Euler angles

q: Why do VR engines track and interpolate head/hand rotation using quaternions instead of Euler angles?
options: Quaternions avoid gimbal lock and interpolate smoothly via SLERP
Quaternions use less memory than any other representation
Euler angles cannot represent 3D rotation at all
Quaternions eliminate the need for a coordinate system
explanation: Quaternions avoid gimbal lock and interpolate smoothly via SLERP

q: What does SLERP stand for in the context of quaternion interpolation?
options: Static Linear Estimation and Rotation Processing
Simple Latency Elimination via Rotation Prediction
explanation: Spherical Linear Interpolation

q: In Unity/Unreal, how do most developers actually construct and interpolate quaternions?
options: By manually deriving 4-component math each frame
Using built-in functions like Quaternion.Slerp() rather than hand-building them
By converting them to plain integers first
explanation: Using built-in functions like Quaternion.Slerp() rather than hand-building them

q: Stereoscopic rendering creates depth perception by:
options: Rendering the scene once and duplicating the image for both eyes
Rendering the scene twice, from two eye-offset virtual cameras separated by IPD
Rendering only for the dominant eye
explanation: Rendering the scene twice, from two eye-offset virtual cameras separated by IPD

q: IPD stands for:
explanation: Interpupillary Distance

q: The average human IPD referenced in the course is approximately:
explanation: 63mm

q: An incorrectly configured IPD (too wide or narrow) is a leading cause of:
options: Eye strain and a 'toy town' or oversized-object feeling
explanation: Eye strain and a 'toy town' or oversized-object feeling

q: Which of these correctly matches an engine to its coordinate convention?
options: Unity: left-handed, Y-up; Unreal: left-handed, Z-up
Unity: right-handed, Z-up; Unreal: left-handed, Y-up
Unity: left-handed, X-up; Unreal: right-handed, Y-up
Both use identical right-handed, Z-up systems
explanation: Unity: left-handed, Y-up; Unreal: left-handed, Z-up

q: Why is recognizing 'why engines default to quaternions for head tracking' called a common conceptual question?
options: Because it is asked in casual conversation only
Because it tests understanding of gimbal lock avoidance and smooth interpolation, not manual math skill
Because quaternions are rarely used in real engines
Because it relates only to audio processing
explanation: Because it tests understanding of gimbal lock avoidance and smooth interpolation, not manual math skill

q: A HandFollow script that copies transform.position and transform.rotation from a tracked hand each frame demonstrates:
options: A simple direct pose-copy from a tracked controller to a game object
explanation: A simple direct pose-copy from a tracked controller to a game object

q: Which statement about depth perception in VR is accurate?
options: Depth comes mainly from rendering the same image to both eyes
Depth comes largely from two horizontally offset camera views matching IPD
Depth is generated purely through audio cues
Depth requires no stereoscopic rendering at all
explanation: Depth comes largely from two horizontally offset camera views matching IPD

q: Porting VR code from an engine that uses right-handed coordinates to one using left-handed coordinates without adjustment would most likely cause:
options: Incorrect object orientations or mirrored transforms
explanation: Incorrect object orientations or mirrored transforms

q: Which best explains why Euler angles are described as 'intuitive but risky' for VR rotation tracking?
options: They are easy to understand but can suffer from gimbal lock
They require no computation at all
They are only usable in 2D games
explanation: They are easy to understand but can suffer from gimbal lock

q: A held virtual weapon that moves perfectly with the player's hand as they walk around the room is most likely implemented using:
options: A weapon parented to the XR camera rig's hand transform
A fixed weapon position unrelated to hand tracking
explanation: A weapon parented to the XR camera rig's hand transform

q: Which of the following would NOT typically be part of a Transform in a VR tracking context?
options: Both position and rotation together define the pose
explanation: Frame rate value

q: What is the primary reason stereoscopic rendering doubles per-frame rendering cost compared to a flat monitor game?
options: The scene must be rendered twice, once per eye, from offset camera positions
VR requires two separate game engines running simultaneously
Stereoscopic rendering has nothing to do with cost
explanation: The scene must be rendered twice, once per eye, from offset camera positions

q: XRI is the abbreviation used in the course for:
explanation: XR Interaction Toolkit

q: Which XRI component lives on the hand/controller and initiates interactions like hovering or grabbing?
explanation: Interactor

q: Which XRI component lives on the object being picked up and defines how it responds to being hovered, selected, or activated?
explanation: Interactable

q: Which of these is NOT listed as a ready-made XRI component in the course?
explanation: XR Audio Mixer

q: What is the primary benefit of using XRI's ready-made components?
options: Developers rarely need to write raw input-polling code for standard interaction patterns
It removes the need for any headset hardware
It automatically writes game narrative content
It disables all physics in the scene
explanation: Developers rarely need to write raw input-polling code for standard interaction patterns

q: To make an object grabbable in Unity's XRI workflow, which steps are described?
options: Add a Rigidbody + Collider, then add an XR Grab Interactable component, and set Movement Type to Kinematic for solid objects
Write a custom physics engine from scratch
Attach only an Audio Source component
explanation: Add a Rigidbody + Collider, then add an XR Grab Interactable component, and set Movement Type to Kinematic for solid objects

q: For custom grab behavior, such as a lever that only rotates on one axis, the course recommends:
options: Rewriting the entire grab logic from scratch
Hooking into XRI's events (e.g., OnSelectEntered) instead of rewriting grab logic
Disabling the XR Grab Interactable entirely
Using only Blueprints, since C# cannot handle events
explanation: Hooking into XRI's events (e.g., OnSelectEntered) instead of rewriting grab logic

q: In the LeverSound example script, OnSelectEntered is wired to which kind of event?
options: A UnityEvent from the Interactable's 'Select Entered' event
explanation: A UnityEvent from the Interactable's 'Select Entered' event

q: Why do most Unity VR apps default to teleportation locomotion rather than smooth joystick movement?
options: Smooth locomotion has a higher risk of triggering motion sickness
Teleportation is required by app store policy
Joysticks are unsupported in VR hardware
explanation: Smooth locomotion has a higher risk of triggering motion sickness

q: In XRI's teleportation workflow, the user typically:
options: Presses a button to instantly appear at a random location
Points a curved ray at the floor, previews a landing reticle, then releases to reposition
Must walk the entire physical distance in real life
Uses only voice commands to move
explanation: Points a curved ray at the floor, previews a landing reticle, then releases to reposition

q: Which pair of XRI components handles teleportation automatically once configured?
options: XR Grab Interactable and XR Ray Interactor
explanation: Teleportation Provider and Teleportation Area

q: To enable teleportation on a floor mesh in XRI, a developer should:
options: Tag the floor mesh as a Teleportation Area
Convert the floor into an XR Grab Interactable
Attach a haptic actuator to the floor
explanation: Tag the floor mesh as a Teleportation Area

q: Why must flat Canvas UI be switched to World Space render mode for VR?
options: So hand rays can interact with buttons floating in 3D space, since there is no mouse cursor in VR
So the UI becomes invisible to the user
So the UI can only be triggered by keyboard shortcuts
World Space mode is required for audio playback
explanation: So hand rays can interact with buttons floating in 3D space, since there is no mouse cursor in VR

q: Which component allows hand rays to click on buttons floating in 3D space in a VR scene?
explanation: XR UI Input Module

q: Which of these best distinguishes Interactor from Interactable in XRI?
options: Interactor lives on the hand and initiates; Interactable lives on the object and responds
Interactor lives on the object; Interactable lives on the hand
They are the same component with different names
Interactor is used only for audio, Interactable only for visuals
explanation: Interactor lives on the hand and initiates; Interactable lives on the object and responds

q: An XR Ray Interactor is most useful for:
options: Interacting with distant objects or UI via a pointing ray
explanation: Interacting with distant objects or UI via a pointing ray

q: What does setting Movement Type to Kinematic on a grabbable object typically achieve?
options: Makes solid grabbed objects behave predictably when held, rather than being fully physics-driven
Prevents the object from ever being grabbed
explanation: Makes solid grabbed objects behave predictably when held, rather than being fully physics-driven

q: Which XRI prefab gives a developer a tracked head camera and two tracked hand controllers in one step?
explanation: XR Origin (VR)
